T9A01: A beam antenna (such as a Yagi) concentrates its signal in one direction, giving gain in that direction and reducing signals from other directions.
T9A02: Loading means electrically lengthening an antenna, for example by adding inductors (loading coils) in the radiating elements. A physically short antenna can then resonate at a lower frequency.
T9A03: An antenna's polarization is described by the orientation of its electric field. A vertical antenna is vertically polarized.
T9A04: A handheld's short 'rubber duck' antenna is much smaller than a full quarter-wave, so it has low efficiency. More of your power is wasted and less is radiated.
T9A05: Shorter antennas resonate at higher frequencies. Shortening a dipole increases its resonant frequency. Lengthening it, or adding coils or capacitive loading, lowers it.
T9A06: A Yagi is a directional beam antenna with multiple elements, so it offers the most gain of these choices. An isotropic antenna is a theoretical reference with zero gain.
T9A07: A vehicle's metal body acts as a shield. Using a handheld inside the car greatly reduces your signal strength. An externally mounted antenna solves this.
T9A08: A quarter-wave on 2 meters is about 19 inches long (1/4 × 2 m ≈ 0.5 m ≈ 19.5 in). A 19-inch vertical is therefore a resonant quarter-wave antenna.
T9A09: A 5/8-wave whip has more gain than a 1/4-wave, because it concentrates more of its energy at low radiation angles toward the horizon, where the other stations are.
T9A10: A half-wave dipole radiates most strongly broadside to the antenna (perpendicular to the wire) and very little off its ends.
T9A11: Antenna gain is the increase in signal strength in a specified direction compared to a reference antenna (such as a dipole or isotropic antenna). An antenna doesn't add power; it focuses it.
T9B01: PL-259, BNC, and Type N connectors all need weather protection outdoors. None of them are fully waterproof on their own, so tape or sealant them.
T9B02: 50 ohms is the most common impedance for coax used in amateur radio, matching the output of most transceivers.
T9B03: Coax is popular because it's easy to use: it can be run next to metal or buried, needs few special installation considerations, and connects easily. It's not the lowest-loss feed line.
T9B04: An antenna tuner matches the antenna system's impedance to the transceiver's output impedance (usually 50 ohms), so the radio sees a low SWR and delivers full power.
T9B05: Coax loss increases as frequency increases. That's why low-loss cable matters more on UHF than on HF.
T9B06: The Type N connector works well above 400 MHz: it has a constant impedance and is more weather resistant. The PL-259 is not suitable for UHF and microwave.
T9B07: PL-259 connectors are commonly used at HF and VHF. They're not watertight, not good for microwaves, and they screw on rather than use a bayonet mount (that's BNC).
T9B08: Water getting into connectors, high SWR, and multiple connectors all add loss in a coax feed line.
T9B09: A loose connection in the antenna or feed line causes erratic, jumping SWR readings, since the connection makes and breaks contact.
T9B10: RG-213 is a thicker cable than RG-58, so it has less loss at a given frequency and handles more power.
T9B11: Air-insulated hardline has the lowest loss of these choices, since air is a nearly perfect dielectric. It's rigid and expensive, though.
T9B12: SWR (standing wave ratio) measures how well the load (antenna) is matched to the transmission line. 1:1 is a perfect match.
T0A01: A 12 V battery won't shock you, but it can deliver huge current. Shorting its terminals (with a wrench, for example) can cause burns, fire, or even an explosion.
T0A02: Electric current through the body can heat tissue (burns), disrupt the electrical function of cells (including the heart), and cause involuntary muscle contractions. All are hazards.
T0A03: In US 120 V AC wiring, black is hot, white is neutral, and green (or bare) is the equipment ground.
T0A04: A fuse removes power in case of an overload: it melts (blows) when the current exceeds its rating, protecting wiring and equipment from overheating.
T0A05: A 20 A fuse would allow up to four times the current the circuit was designed for. Wiring could overheat and cause a fire before the fuse blows. Always replace fuses with the same rating.
T0A06: Using three-wire grounded cords, bonding equipment to a common safety ground, and discharging high-voltage capacitors before working inside equipment all protect against shock.
T0A07: A lightning arrester belongs on a grounded panel near where the feed lines enter the building, so lightning energy is diverted to ground before it gets inside.
T0A08: A fuse or circuit breaker goes in series with the hot conductor only. Fusing the neutral could leave the equipment 'hot' even after the fuse opens.
T0A09: All external ground rods must be bonded together with heavy wire or strap. This keeps everything at the same potential and prevents dangerous voltage differences during a lightning strike.
T0A10: Charging or discharging an unprotected battery too fast can cause overheating or out-gassing (releasing flammable or toxic gases). Lithium batteries can even catch fire.
T0A11: Power supply filter capacitors can hold a dangerous charge even after the power is turned off. Always discharge them before touching anything inside.
T0A12: When measuring high voltages, make sure the meter and its leads are rated for that voltage. Underrated equipment can arc over and expose you to the voltage.
T0B01: Ground connections for lightning protection should be short and direct. Lightning current doesn't like sharp bends; it may jump off the wire. Avoid drip loops in grounds.
T0B02: Tower climbing requires proper training, being tied off to the tower at all times, and wearing an approved climbing harness.
T0B03: Never climb a tower without a helper or observer, no matter how low or simple the job is. Someone needs to be able to get help if something goes wrong.
T0B04: When putting up a tower or antenna, look for and stay clear of overhead power lines. Contact with power lines is one of the leading causes of ham radio deaths.
T0B05: A safety wire through a turnbuckle keeps it from loosening (unscrewing) due to vibration from wind.
T0B06: Place antennas far enough from power lines that if the antenna fell, no part of it could come within 10 feet of the power wires.
T0B07: Never climb a crank-up tower unless it's fully retracted or has mechanical safety locks installed. A cable failure could drop the sections suddenly.
T0B08: Proper tower grounding uses separate 8-foot ground rods for each tower leg, bonded to the tower and to each other.
T0B09: Never attach an antenna to a utility pole. It could contact high-voltage power lines, and it's also not your pole.
T0B10: Lightning protection ground conductors should avoid sharp bends, because lightning current tends to jump off the wire at sharp corners.
T0B11: Local electrical codes (often based on the National Electrical Code) establish grounding requirements for towers and antennas, not FCC Part 97.
T0C01: Radio signals are non-ionizing radiation: they don't have enough energy to knock electrons off atoms. X-rays and gamma rays are ionizing.
T0C02: The human body absorbs RF most efficiently around 30-300 MHz (VHF), where the body is resonant. So exposure limits are lowest (strictest) in that range. Of the choices, 50 MHz falls in this range.
T0C03: Exposure limits are averaged over time. At a 50% duty cycle, you transmit half as much, so the allowed power density doubles (increases by a factor of 2).
T0C04: RF exposure depends on frequency and power level, the distance from the antenna, and the antenna's radiation pattern. All are factors.
T0C05: Exposure limits vary with frequency because the human body absorbs RF energy more at some frequencies than others (body resonance).
T0C06: You may determine compliance by calculation using FCC OET Bulletin 65, by computer modeling, or by measuring field strength with calibrated equipment. All are acceptable.
T0C07: Touching an antenna during transmission can cause an RF burn to the skin. RF is non-ionizing radiation, and electrocution is not the typical hazard at amateur power levels.
T0C08: Moving antennas farther from people (or higher) reduces RF exposure. Moving the transmitter doesn't matter, since the antenna is what radiates, and increasing duty cycle increases exposure.
T0C09: Re-evaluate your station's RF exposure whenever you change the transmitter, power, or antenna system. You don't need to notify the FCC.
T0C10: Duty cycle (how much of the time you transmit) affects average exposure, which is what the RF safety limits are based on.
T0C11: Duty cycle is the percentage of time a transmitter is transmitting during the averaging period. For example, transmitting half the time is a 50% duty cycle.
T0C12: RF radiation does not have enough energy to cause chemical changes in cells or damage DNA, unlike ionizing radiation. However, it can heat tissue, so it is not 'perfectly safe.'
T0C13: The station licensee is responsible for ensuring that nobody is exposed to RF energy above the FCC limits.
